claims.text: A controlled minor similar-element substitution that narrows the atomic-size distribution can improve glass-forming ability in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
The proposed substitution can enhance the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous state.
Rapidly cooled phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys yield a partially amorphous structure.
The initial partially amorphous structure has significant lattice distortion.
Replacing one transition metal with a chemically similar element having a slightly different atomic radius can tune the δ′ parameter.
The beneficial effect is expected at minor substitution levels below 10% when the replacement has similar chemical behavior.
The expected benefits may not occur under slow-cooling conditions.
The expected benefits may not occur at high substitution levels.
The substitution produces reduced lattice distortion and a more uniform atomic-size distribution in the amorphous matrix.
Lower lattice distortion decreases the density of heterogeneous nucleation sites for crystallization.
A lower density of heterogeneous nucleation sites stabilizes the amorphous structure during thermal exposure.
Adjusting interatomic spacing diminishes the driving force for phase separation.
The modified alloy will have a broader processing window for obtaining a fully amorphous state than the unsubstituted baseline.
The modified alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the unsubstituted baseline.
Excessive substitution or an inappropriate replacement element could negate the benefit or promote crystallization.
